newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative govt dismisses pension criticism.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative govt dismisses pension criticism.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservative party on Wednesday dismissed opposition charges that its plans for a pension "revolution" would cost the taxpayer 151 billion pounds ($243.5 billion) by the year 2040.

Due to changes in pension law already enacted and due to come into effect after the year 2000, the scheme would more than pay for itself, providing significant savings by the year 2025, senior Conservative party and official sources said.
Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown accused Major on Wednesday of wanting to privatise state pensions.

Brown said the cumulative public cost of the scheme would reach 151 billion pounds by the year 2040 which would have to be funded through tax rises, even without setting aside money to guarantee basic pensions if private funds failed.
But the sources rejected the charge that the basic pension would disappear, saying the scheme would guarantee that everyone received a pension equivalent to the basic state provision.
They also dismissed Labour's charge that the cost would reach 151 billion pounds. "This is a bit of a propaganda trick," said one senior Conservative party source.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury William Waldegrave told parliament's Treasury Select Committee on Wednesday that there was a cost in funding the change between systems, but said the burden was not intolerable.
A Department of Social Security spokesman said although there were initial costs, the scheme in the end saved money.
"And of course the great thing is that you have broken the cycle. You have done what no other industrial nation has done and changed to a funded pension system," the spokesman said.

The sources said equalising the age at which men and women are entitled to a state pension at 65, instead of the current entitlement for 60 for women and 65 for men, would produce savings rising to six billion pounds annually by the year 2025.

Another reform restricting entitlement to the state earnings-related pension scheme (SERPS), which provides a second pension to about 6.5 million people, will produce savings rising to a total of seven billion pounds annually by the year 2040.

The sources said there were transitional costs of seven billion pounds which were included in the proposals. But, taken together with the savings from the changes already enacted, the new scheme would in the end cut public spending, they said.
The proposals announced by Major on Wednesday are aimed at preventing huge burdens falling on future taxpayers by making workers take responsibility for providing for their old age.

"This will put us another huge step ahead -- enabling us to sustain a healthy, low-tax economy for the future," said Major, unveiling complex proposals under which every individual would build up a personal fund to provide an income on retirement. ($1=.6202 Pound)
The FT said opposition Labour called on the government to make a statement in the House of Commons to explain its actions.
